newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia trade pacts with Europe still far off.
newsitem.headline: Croatia trade pacts with Europe still far off.

text.p: Membership of the Council of Europe may bring Croatia a step closer to the European Union (EU) but stronger trade and financial ties with the bloc may still be a long way off, analysts said on Wednesday.

"Croatia is prepared to discuss and negotiate but much will depend on the political will of the European Commission," said a Chamber of Economy source who asked not to be named. "So far, it has often kicked the ball off-court."

Prime Minister Zlatko Matesa hailed news that the Council of Europe voted to admit Croatia as a member, but was quoted as saying this was only "an essential first step in the process of full integration into a community of European states".
An agreement on trade and cooperation with Europe was put on ice almost two years ago over the government's alleged human rights abuses and criticism of its democratic record.
Although Croatia has continued trading with Western countries after gaining independence from the former Yugoslavia, the country has yet to be granted more favourable terms of trade by the EU.

Its patchy record on democratic issues has also blocked its access to all technical assistance, including the so-called PHARE programme of support for reforms in post-communist states, and vital investments.
"There may be no funds from PHARE until 1998 as the budget for next year has already been determined," a source close to the government said.
But political and economic analysts agreed membership in the Council may provide a "carrot" for the government to speed up the pace of overall reforms.

While admitting Europe was unlikely to open any investment taps immediately, they said it would over time probably funnel more funds to the private sector to enable a higher degree of financial independence from the state.
Croatia would still be expected to reshuffle its political system and pass missing legislation, including an anti-monopoly law, to spur the development of a free market economy.

"But the only way to future integration are bilateral customs agreements with CEFTA (Central Europe Free Trade Association) countries," said Davor Gjenero. He said Croatia could join CEFTA within two years.
